config.title: useDebounce

intro.title: useDebounce
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build debounced search behavior in a React component: the UI shows what you type immediately, while a separate value updates only after you pause typing. You will implement this with useState and useEffect (and TypeScript), using setTimeout and clearTimeout so rapid keystrokes reset the timer. By the end, you will see live vs debounced values side by side — the same pattern used for search boxes and API calls that should not fire on every keypress.
intro.usecase: Debounced input is essential where real-time typing must not trigger work on every keystroke. E‑commerce search, dashboard filters, and username availability checks typically wait until the user pauses before fetching or validating, keeping the app responsive and reducing load on servers and clients.

objectives: Write a custom hook useDebounce<T>(value: T, delay: number): T with explicit input and return types so the abstraction solves a concrete UI lesson and exposes a reliable typed contract.

Model a useState<T> variable for the debounced value initialized to the input value so state, refs, or values keep a predictable shape as the feature evolves, and data shape and updates remain explicit throughout the lesson.

Use useEffect with a setTimeout to update the debounced state and return a clearTimeout cleanup so the pattern drives visible behavior, and the effect leaves no stale subscriptions, timers, or listeners behind.
Consume useDebounce in a search component and demonstrate that the API call fires only after the delay so the learner can connect the typed API to real screen behavior.

steps.title: Initialize state for the search input value
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, declare a state variable named 'searchTerm' and its setter using useState. Initialize it as an empty string with TypeScript typing.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook you imported earlier. Remember to provide the type annotation for the state variable (string).
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: initializing a string state
const [username, setUsername] = useState<string>('');
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component now has a searchTerm state variable initialized to an empty string with proper TypeScript typing.
successCriteria: searchTerm state is declared using useState with an empty string initial value and string type annotation
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using useState with an empty string initial value and specifying the string type.
steps.feedbackWrong: Declare a state variable named searchTerm using useState, initialized as an empty string with TypeScript typing.

steps.title: Initialize state for the debounced value
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, declare **`debouncedTerm`** and **`setDebouncedTerm`** with **`useState`**, initialized to an empty string and typed as **`string`**: e.g. **`const [debouncedTerm, setDebouncedTerm] = useState<string>('');`**. This holds the value that updates only after typing pauses (you will wire the delay in **`useEffect`** next).
steps.hint: Mirror your `searchTerm` pattern: a tuple from `useState`, generic `string`, initial value `''`.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component has a debouncedTerm state variable (and setter) ready for the debounce effect to update.
successCriteria: debouncedTerm and setDebouncedTerm are declared with useState, empty string initial value, and string typing.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Add `const [debouncedTerm, setDebouncedTerm] = useState<string>('');` (or equivalent) after your searchTerm state.
steps.feedbackWrong: Declare debounced state: `const [debouncedTerm, setDebouncedTerm] = useState<string>('');` inside App.

steps.title: Implement the debounce logic with useEffect
steps.instruction: Add a useEffect inside App that runs when **`searchTerm`** changes: schedule **`setDebouncedTerm(searchTerm)`** (or equivalent) after **500ms** using **`setTimeout`**, and **`return`** a cleanup function that **`clearTimeout`** on the timer you created (store the timer id in a **local** `const` inside the effect, e.g. `const timerId = setTimeout(...)`).
steps.hint: Dependencies must include searchTerm. Cleanup runs when searchTerm changes or on unmount — always clear the pending timeout so an old timer cannot update state after a new keystroke.
steps.expectedOutcome: A useEffect debounces updates to debouncedTerm using setTimeout, searchTerm as a dependency, and clearTimeout in the cleanup function.
successCriteria: useEffect depends on searchTerm, uses setTimeout to call setDebouncedTerm after 500ms, and returns a cleanup that clearTimeout the scheduled timer.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check: searchTerm in the dependency array, setTimeout → setDebouncedTerm, and return () => clearTimeout(timerId).
steps.feedbackWrong: You need a useEffect with [searchTerm], setTimeout(…, 500) updating debounced state, and cleanup with clearTimeout.

steps.title: Create the search input handler function
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, create a function named 'handleSearchChange' that takes a React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> as a parameter and updates the searchTerm state with the input's current value.
steps.hint: Define a function that receives an event parameter, extracts event.target.value, and calls setSearchTerm with that value.
steps.expectedOutcome: A typed event handler function that updates the searchTerm state when called with an input change event.
successCriteria: The handleSearchChange function is defined, takes a React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> parameter, and calls setSearchTerm with event.target.value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a function, but check that it properly extracts the value from the event and updates the searchTerm state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function isn't defined correctly. Make sure it's named handleSearchChange, accepts a React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> parameter, and calls setSearchTerm with the input value.

steps.instruction: Inside your component's return statement, add an input element with type='text', value bound to searchTerm, and onChange wired to handleSearchChange.
steps.hint: Use JSX syntax for the input element. The value attribute should be set to the searchTerm state variable, and the onChange event handler should call handleSearchChange.

<input type="text" value={inputValue} onChange={handleChange} />
steps.expectedOutcome: The JSX now includes a controlled input element that updates the searchTerm state when the user types.
successCriteria: An input element with type='text', value={searchTerm}, and onChange={handleSearchChange} is present in the return statement.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the input element has all three required attributes: type='text', value={searchTerm}, and onChange={handleSearchChange}.
